titre: Paris au XXe siècle (Paris in the Twentieth Century), the Novel Verne Never Saw Published
accroche: Verne offers his publisher a very dark novel about the Paris of 1960; Hetzel turns it down, and it appears only in 1994, more than a century after it was written.
contenu_vulgarise:
## A Novel Too Dark for Its Time

Verne wrote *Paris au XXe siècle* (*Paris in the Twentieth Century*) in 1860, not in 1863 as critics had first supposed. After reworking it, he offered it to his publisher, Pierre-Jules Hetzel, after the publication of *Cinq semaines en ballon* (*Five Weeks in a Balloon*) in 1863 and before the start of the serialization of *Les Aventures du capitaine Hatteras* (*The Adventures of Captain Hatteras*). It is the story of a young man, Michel Dufrénoy, winner of a prize for Latin poetry, in a Paris of 1960 where science has triumphed and where literature, music, and painting are despised.

## The Rejection, Then More Than a Century of Silence

Hetzel turned down this very dark novel of anticipation on the grounds that it would harm the author's reputation, and added: “No one today will believe your prophecies.” According to the English version of Wikipedia, Hetzel even advised him to wait twenty years before publishing. Verne, then a young author, followed his advice and abandoned the project. The text resurfaced only in 1989, when the writer's great-grandson found the manuscript, annotated by Hetzel, in a safe in the family home in Toulon. It was published in 1994 by Hachette and Le Cherche midi jointly, in an edition prepared by Piero Gondolo della Riva, with illustrations by François Schuiten.

## What the “Visionary” Verne Hides

The Paris that Verne imagines is nothing like a technological utopia. Subway trains driven by compressed air, hydrogen-powered cars, and machines resembling photocopiers and computers stand alongside a world where war has become so scientific that soldiers are no longer needed, and so effective that it is inconceivable. Michel looks for Hugo and Balzac, but the bookshops now offer only books on technology, and his collection of poems, *Espoirs* (*Hopes*), is rejected by every publisher in the city. Verne also anticipates the growth of motorized traffic, the formation of suburbs, the abandonment of Greek and Latin in schools, music that is no longer sung but screamed, and the influence of English on French. The book contains this sentence: “Everyone grows rich, except the human spirit.” Wikipedia sees in it a very pessimistic Verne, a pessimism he kept hidden all his life and which resurfaced only in his last novels: the novel remained unpublished until 1994.

repere.texte: Written in 1860 and offered to Hetzel after Cinq semaines en ballon (1863), the manuscript of Paris au XXe siècle was rejected, abandoned by Verne, found in 1989 in a safe in the family home in Toulon, and published only in 1994, more than a century after it was written.

carte.punch: Verne wrote a novel so dark that his publisher turned it down: it appeared only in 1994.
carte.idee: Hetzel rejects Paris au XXe siècle, a very dark novel of anticipation, on the grounds that it would harm Verne's reputation. The manuscript, annotated by the publisher, is found in 1989 in a safe in Toulon by the writer's great-grandson, and appears only in 1994.

quiz.question: Why does Hetzel reject Paris au XXe siècle?
choix: He lacks room in his catalog for a new Verne series that year
The text contains scientific errors that he judges too glaring to publish
He fears that such a pessimistic novel would harm Verne's reputation
He finds it too optimistic about the future to appeal to Verne's readers
quiz.explication: Hetzel rejects this very dark novel on the grounds that it would harm the author's reputation: “No one today will believe your prophecies.”

quiz_supplementaire.question: How is the manuscript of Paris au XXe siècle found?
choix: In Hetzel's personal archives, bequeathed to the Bibliothèque nationale de France
In a safe in the family home in Toulon, by Verne's great-grandson, in 1989
At a Paris bookseller who had bought it without knowing it was unpublished
In the papers of an American translator who was preparing a posthumous edition
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The author's great-grandson finds the manuscript in 1989 in a safe in the family home in Toulon; it appears in 1994.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Paris of 1960 imagined by Verne actually describe?
choix: A technological utopia where the arts flourish thanks to machines
A military dictatorship that has abolished all forms of commerce
A return to rural life after the abandonment of the big cities
A utilitarian society where literature and poetry no longer interest anyone
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Verne describes a world where “everyone grows rich, except the human spirit”: the bookshops offer only books on technology, and the hero's collection of poems is rejected by every publisher.
